clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic SUMF1 variants; SUMF1 encodes the formylglycine-generating enzyme (FGE) that post-translationally activates every human sulfatase.
Because a single defect cripples all sulfatases simultaneously, the phenotype blends metachromatic leukodystrophy, several mucopolysaccharidoses, X-linked ichthyosis and chondrodysplasia punctata.

Suspect the diagnosis whenever a child shows features of more than one sulfatase-deficiency disorder at once — for example neuroregression together with coarse features, skeletal change and ichthyosis.
Ichthyosis (from steroid sulfatase deficiency) coexisting with a leukodystrophy-like decline is a particularly useful pointer away from isolated metachromatic leukodystrophy.
The neurological picture resembles metachromatic leukodystrophy — developmental regression, spasticity and a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy — but is broader.
Additional features include hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, coarse facies, deafness and, in some, corneal clouding and cardiac involvement.
Diagnosis is supported by finding reduced activity across several sulfatases in leucocytes or fibroblasts, then confirmed by SUMF1 sequencing.
A clinical spectrum exists from a severe neonatal MPS-like form to late-infantile (most common) and juvenile presentations.
reference.pathophysiology: SUMF1 encodes the formylglycine-generating enzyme (FGE), which resides in the endoplasmic reticulum and carries out an obligatory post-translational modification of newly synthesised sulfatases, oxidising a conserved cysteine residue within their active site to Cα-formylglycine. This modified residue is essential for catalytic activity, so a single deficient FGE inactivates the entire family of human sulfatases. The resulting global loss of sulfatase function impairs degradation of sulfated substrates throughout the body: sulfatides accumulate in central and peripheral myelin (as in metachromatic leukodystrophy), glycosaminoglycans accumulate in lysosomes and connective tissue (as in the mucopolysaccharidoses), cholesterol sulfate accumulates in the epidermis (producing ichthyosis), and defective arylsulfatase E activity disturbs cartilage and bone development (chondrodysplasia punctata). The convergence of lysosomal storage, dysmyelination and impaired epidermal and skeletal turnover produces the combined multisystem, neurodegenerative phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Individual mucopolysaccharidoses, particularly types II, III, IVA and VI
GM1 gangliosidosis and other lysosomal storage disorders with coarse features
Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders with combined neurological and skeletal features
additionalInvestigations: Enzyme assays of multiple sulfatases in leucocytes or cultured fibroblasts, showing generalised reduction
SUMF1 gene sequencing for definitive confirmation
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy
Brain MRI showing a leukodystrophy pattern with white-matter signal change
Skeletal survey for dysostosis multiplex and chondrodysplasia punctata
redFlags: Developmental regression with loss of previously acquired milestones
Neurological decline occurring together with ichthyosis or coarsening facial features
Rapidly progressive spasticity or bulbar dysfunction
New sensorineural hearing loss alongside multisystem involvement
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive with a generally poor outlook; the severe neonatal form is often fatal in early childhood, and the more common late-infantile form leads to relentless neurological deterioration over a few years after onset. No curative therapy is available and care is supportive.
pitfalls: Diagnosing only one component such as metachromatic leukodystrophy and missing the unifying combined disorder
Assuming several independent diagnoses rather than a single SUMF1 defect
Confusing reduced arylsulfatase A activity with common arylsulfatase A pseudodeficiency
Overlooking subtle ichthyosis or skeletal changes that would point to the combined phenotype
Relying on a single sulfatase assay rather than testing several enzymes when the disorder is suspected
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts (standard reference)
Lysosomal storage disorder clinical references (standard reference)
management: No curative or enzyme-replacement therapy exists; care is supportive and directed at the individual manifestations

Neurological supportive care mirroring metachromatic leukodystrophy, with antispasticity agents such as baclofen, management of the demyelinating neuropathy and physiotherapy for progressive spasticity
Seizure control with antiepileptic drugs where epilepsy develops
Skin care with emollients and keratolytics for the ichthyosis arising from steroid sulfatase deficiency
Nutritional support, including gastrostomy feeding for dysphagia, alongside airway and respiratory care
Surveillance and management of the mucopolysaccharidosis-like features, with hearing aids for deafness, ophthalmic review for corneal clouding and cardiac assessment
Autosomal recessive SUMF1 genetic counselling with family testing, and early palliative-care involvement given the progressive course
